data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":{"adopted_commitment_refs":[],"disanalogies":["SRC_008 discusses a continuous outcome space and high-dimensional features; here the outcome is objectively verifiable, which may simplify the structure and reduce the penalty of dimensionality reduction.","SRC_008 frames information loss as a model property; here the information loss is procedural\u2014a deliberate design choice in the checklist.","The panel in this problem aggregates multiple non-experts, which can partially recover information lost by individual checklist compliance through stochastic variation in interpretation, whereas SRC_008 does not involve ensemble averaging."],"overturn_conditions":["If empirical evaluation shows the panel outperforming the expert on adversarial items designed to break the checklist, the dimensionality-reduction framing is insufficient.","If the expert's intuition is shown to be a low-dimensional heuristic masquerading as high-dimensional reasoning, the analogy to SRC_008's information-rich high-dimensional space fails.","If the aggregation of non-experts is shown to recover information not present in the checklist via emergent collective intelligence, the bottleneck model is incomplete."],"shared_structure":["Both involve a structural bottleneck: SRC_008's argument about dimensionality reduction and information loss mirrors the checklist's projection from the expert's high-dimensional feature space to a low-dimensional checklist space.","Both depend on task structure: the severity of information loss in SRC_008 depends on the outcome space's topology, just as the checklist's fidelity depends on the outcome-determination function's complexity.","In both, the apparent advantage of the reduced system (panel/checklist or the reduced model) is conditional on the sufficiency of the retained dimensions."],"source_memory_refs":["SRC_008","SRC_001"],"transfer_claims":["SRC_008's argument that dimensionality reduction causes information loss transfers directly: the checklist is a dimensionality-reduction tool, and its reliability gain is bounded by the information retained.","The condition under which the panel wins is the same as the condition under which SRC_008's 'against' case weakens: when the outcome is determined by a structure that the reduced representation (checklist) captures fully.","The diagnostic for distinguishing genuine reliability from compliance tracking\u2014testing on items where the reduced representation is misleading\u2014transfers from SRC_008's logic of probing the high-dimensional space with cases the low-dimensional model gets wrong."]},"claim":"The checklist's apparent reliability advantage is a separability artifact: it transfers reliability gains only in task regions where the checklist items correspond one-to-one with the objectively-verifiable outcome structure. Single experts capture latent cues the checklist ignores, so panel reliability collapses exactly when an item's checklist-compliance surface and its outcome-determination surface diverge. An evaluation distinguishes a genuine reliability gain from mere compliance tracking by testing on adversarially-constructed items where checklist compliance is achievable by a misleading subset of features.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the expert's intuition is systematically biased (e.g., overweighting salient but non-diagnostic cues), the checklist's information loss is beneficial, and the panel will outperform the expert even outside the checklist subspace.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the task outcome is truly determined by a small, linear, non-interacting set of features, the checklist projection is information-preserving and the panel will match or exceed the expert without any subspace collapse.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the expert's 'intuition' is actually a well-rehearsed internal checklist, the dichotomy between checklist and intuition is false and the panel's only advantage is aggregation noise reduction.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"A checklist defines a low-dimensional projection of the outcome-determining feature space. Trained non-experts using it will reliably produce correct answers only when that projection is information-preserving with respect to the outcome class. A domain expert relies on intuition, which is a high-dimensional model encoding latent feature combinations that the checklist eliminates. The panel's reliability gain is genuine only within the task subspace spanned by the checklist. Outside it, the panel exhibits high agreement (because all members apply the same checklist) but low accuracy, while the expert's variance increases but their mean accuracy degrades less because their implicit model retains more outcome-relevant dimensions. Thus the panel's 'reliability' is often a reliability of process, not of outcome.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
